<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:periodic}
(a) $r$ is even and $4\pi/m$-periodic.
(b) If $a=b$ and $n_2=n_3$, then $r$ is $2\pi/m$-periodic.
(c) Consequently $r$ is $2\pi$-periodic, i.e.\ $\gamma$ closes after one turn, whenever $m$ is even, or $a=b$ and $n_2=n_3$. The curve is then invariant under the reflection in the $x$-axis and under the rotation by $2\pi/K$, where $K=m/2$ in general and $K=m$ in case~(b); it consists of $K$ congruent arcs. If $m$ is odd and (b) fails, then in general $r(\varphi+2\pi)\neq r(\varphi)$ and $\gamma$ closes only after $\varphi$ has run over $[0,4\pi]$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(a) $\varphi\mapsto-\varphi$ leaves $|\cos\frac{m\varphi}{4}|$ and $|\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}|$ unchanged, and $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+4\pi/m$ adds $\pi$ to $m\varphi/4$, which only changes signs. (b) $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+2\pi/m$ adds $\pi/2$ to $m\varphi/4$ and interchanges $|\cos|$ and $|\sin|$. (c) $2\pi=\frac m2\cdot\frac{4\pi}{m}=m\cdot\frac{2\pi}{m}$; evenness of $r$ is the reflection symmetry.
\qed
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:regular}
Away from the zeros of $\sin(m\varphi/2)$ the function $r$ is real-analytic. Let $\varphi_*$ be a zero of $\sin(m\varphi/4)$ and put $n=n_3$, or a zero of $\cos(m\varphi/4)$ and put $n=n_2$. Near $\varphi_*$, $r$ is of class $C^k$ if and only if $|\varphi-\varphi_*|^n$ is; that is, $r$ is $C^\infty$ (indeed real-analytic) near $\varphi_*$ if $n$ is an even integer, and otherwise $r\in C^k$ near $\varphi_*$ exactly for the integers $k<n$. In particular, the exponent $n_1$ has no influence on the regularity of $r$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ denote the bracket in \eqref{eq:gielis}. The two terms of $A$ do not vanish simultaneously, so $A>0$, and $y\mapsto y^{-1/n_1}$ is an analytic diffeomorphism of $(0,\infty)$; hence $r$ and $A$ have the same regularity everywhere, whatever $n_1$. Away from the zeros of $\cos\frac{m\varphi}{4}\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}=\frac12\sin\frac{m\varphi}{2}$ both terms of $A$ are analytic. Near a zero $\varphi_*$ of $\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}$ the first term is analytic, and $\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}=(\varphi-\varphi_*)g(\varphi)$ with $g$ analytic and $g(\varphi_*)=\pm m/4\neq0$, so $|\frac1b\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}|^{n_3}=|\varphi-\varphi_*|^{n_3}h(\varphi)$ with $h$ analytic and positive; multiplication by $h$ preserves the class $C^k$. The same argument applies at the zeros of $\cos\frac{m\varphi}{4}$. Finally, for $x\neq0$ the $k$-th derivative of $|x|^n$ is $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)|x|^{n-k}(\operatorname{sgn}x)^k$. If $n$ is an even integer, $|x|^n=x^n$ is analytic, and so are $A$ and $r$. Otherwise, for $k<n$ this derivative extends continuously to $x=0$ (with value $0$), whereas for the smallest integer $k\ge n$ it is unbounded near $0$ ($n\notin\mathbb Z$) or has a jump at $0$ ($n$ odd); hence $|x|^n\in C^k$ exactly for $k<n$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:geom}
Near a point $\varphi_*$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:regular}, with governing exponent $n$:
if $n\ge2$, then $r\in C^2$ and $\kappa$ is continuous;
if $1<n<2$, the curve is $C^1$ but $\kappa$ is unbounded;
if $n=1$, $r'$ has a jump and $\gamma$ has a corner;
if $0<n<1$, $|r'|\to\infty$ and $\gamma$ has a cusp (the unit tangent tends to the radial direction, with opposite orientations on the two sides).
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Throughout the proof $x=\varphi-\varphi_*$, and the Landau symbols refer to the limit $x\to0$: $O(1)$ denotes a quantity that remains bounded and $o(1)$ a quantity that tends to $0$; $f=O(|x|^q)$ means $|f|\le M|x|^q$ for some constant $M$ and all small $x\neq0$. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:regular}, $A=A_0(\varphi)+|x|^nh(\varphi)$ with $A_0,h$ analytic near $\varphi_*$, $h>0$ and $A_0'(\varphi_*)=0$. Since $r=A^{-1/n_1}$, we have for $x\neq0$
\[
r'=-\tfrac{1}{n_1}A^{-1/n_1-1}A',\qquad
r''=-\tfrac{1}{n_1}A^{-1/n_1-1}A''+\tfrac{1}{n_1}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{n_1}+1\bigr)A^{-1/n_1-2}(A')^2 .
\]

If $n\ge2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:regular} gives $r\in C^2$, so $\kappa$ in \eqref{eq:kappa} is continuous.

Now let $1<n<2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:regular}, $r\in C^1$; in particular $r$ and $r'$ are bounded, and $A'=A_0'+n\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{n-1}h+|x|^nh'=O(1)$. Differentiating once more,
\[
A''=n(n-1)h(\varphi_*)|x|^{n-2}+O(1),
\]
where $O(1)$ collects $A_0''$, $2n\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{n-1}h'$, $|x|^nh''$ and $n(n-1)|x|^{n-2}\bigl(h(\varphi)-h(\varphi_*)\bigr)=O(|x|^{n-1})$, all bounded because $n>1$. The second term in $r''$ is $O(1)$ as well, since $A'=O(1)$ and $A$ is bounded away from $0$. Hence
\[
r''=-\tfrac{1}{n_1}A^{-1/n_1-1}\,n(n-1)h(\varphi_*)\,|x|^{n-2}+O(1).
\]
The first term tends to $\pm\infty$ because $n-2<0$ and $n(n-1)h(\varphi_*)\neq0$; adding a bounded quantity cannot prevent this, so $|r''|\to\infty$. As $r$ and $r'$ are bounded and $r^2+r'^2\ge r^2>0$, $\kappa$ in \eqref{eq:kappa} is unbounded.

If $n=1$, then $A'=A_0'+\operatorname{sgn}(x)h+|x|h'$, and $A_0'(\varphi_*)=0$ gives the one-sided limits $A'(\varphi_*^\pm)=\pm h(\varphi_*)\neq0$. Thus $r'$ has a jump at $\varphi_*$, and so has the direction of $\gamma'=r'\,\mathbf e_r+r\,\mathbf e_\varphi$ (polar frame $\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\varphi$): $\gamma$ has a corner.

Finally, let $0<n<1$. We write
\[
A'=n\operatorname{sgn}(x)h(\varphi_*)|x|^{n-1}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr).
\]
Indeed, the remaining terms $A_0'=O(|x|)$ (because $A_0'(\varphi_*)=0$), $n\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{n-1}\bigl(h(\varphi)-h(\varphi_*)\bigr)=O(|x|^n)$ and $|x|^nh'=O(|x|^n)$ are, relative to $|x|^{n-1}$, of order $O(|x|^{2-n})$, $O(|x|)$ and $O(|x|)$; since $2-n>1$, the relative error is $O(|x|)=o(1)$. Consequently
\[
r'=-\tfrac{1}{n_1}A^{-1/n_1-1}\,n\operatorname{sgn}(x)h(\varphi_*)|x|^{n-1}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr).
\]
For $|x|$ small the factor $1+o(1)$ is positive, so $\operatorname{sgn}(r')=-\operatorname{sgn}(n_1)\operatorname{sgn}(x)$, and $|r'|\to\infty$ because $n-1<0$. (A bounded error term $O(1)$ in place of $o(1)$ would not suffice here: it could reverse the sign of the factor $1+O(1)$.) Therefore
\[
\frac{\gamma'}{|\gamma'|}=\frac{r'\,\mathbf e_r+r\,\mathbf e_\varphi}{\sqrt{r'^2+r^2}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{sgn}(r')\,\mathbf e_r(\varphi_*)=\mp\operatorname{sgn}(n_1)\,\mathbf e_r(\varphi_*)\qquad\text{as }x\to0^\pm ,
\]
so the unit tangent reverses its direction at $\varphi_*$: $\gamma$ has a cusp.
\qed
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:n1}
In the frequently used diagonal case $n_1=n_2=n_3=n$, the condition $n<2$ does produce singular points; by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular} this is due to $n_2$ and $n_3$, not to $n_1$. For example, $(4;1,4,4)$ is real-analytic although $n_1=1$, whereas $(4;4,1,1)$ has corners although $n_1=4$ (both are verified numerically; see Section~\ref{sec:numerics}). This corrects the heuristic, stated for instance in \cite[Abstract and Section~1]{Ozdemir2026}, that small values of $n_1$ ($n_1<2$) create corner-like singularities. All smooth test curves of this paper have $n_2,n_3\in\{4,6,7\}$, hence $r\in C^6$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:fraccurv}
The fractional curvature and torsion along the parameter $s$ are
\[
\kappa_\alpha[s]=\frac{\bigl\langle d\mathbf{t}/ds,\mathbf{n}\bigr\rangle}{|D^\alpha_s x|},\qquad
\tau_\alpha[s]=\frac{\bigl\langle d\mathbf{n}/ds,\mathbf{b}\bigr\rangle}{|D^\alpha_s x|}
\]
(for plane curves $\mathbf{n}$ is $\mathbf{t}$ rotated by $+\pi/2$ and $\kappa_\alpha$ is signed).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:param}
For the quantities of Definition~\ref{def:fraccurv}, $\kappa_\alpha[s]=\kappa(u)/\lambda_\alpha(s(u))$ and $\tau_\alpha[s]=\tau(u)/\lambda_\alpha(s(u))$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$d\mathbf{t}/ds=\kappa\mathbf{n}\,du/ds$, $d\mathbf{n}/ds=(-\kappa\mathbf{t}+\tau\mathbf{b})\,du/ds$ and $|D^\alpha_s x|=\lambda_\alpha(s)\,du/ds$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:HY}
In \cite{HasYilmaz2023} the parameter $s$ is introduced by (2.8), so it is $s_F$ and not the Euclidean arc length; the phrase ``where $s$ measures its arc length'' in their Theorems~2.6--2.7 has to be understood in the sense of unit fractional speed, $\|d^\alpha x/ds^\alpha\|=1$, established after their (2.11). Reading $s$ as Euclidean arc length in (2.13)--(2.14) yields convention~E instead. The two conventions differ by the factor $w_F/w_E=(C_F/C_E)\,u^{(1-\alpha)^2/\alpha}$; for $\alpha=1/2$, for example, $\kappa^E_\alpha=\kappa/(0.5642\,u^{1/2})$ whereas $\kappa^F_\alpha=2\pi\kappa/u$. We state all results for both conventions.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:frenet}
Let $P(u)=\int_0^u w(v)\,dv=C\,u^{p+1}/(p+1)$. With $'=d/dP$ the classical frame satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frenetP}
\mathbf{t}'=\kappa_\alpha\mathbf{n},\qquad \mathbf{n}'=-\kappa_\alpha\mathbf{t}+\tau_\alpha\mathbf{b},\qquad \mathbf{b}'=-\tau_\alpha\mathbf{n} .
\end{equation}
In convention F, $P=s_F$ of \eqref{eq:sF} and \eqref{eq:frenetP} is \cite[eq.~(2.12)]{HasYilmaz2023}; in convention E, $P_E(u)=\alpha u^{2-\alpha}/\Gamma(3-\alpha)$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$d/dP=w^{-1}d/du$, the classical Frenet equations and \eqref{eq:scaling}.
\qed
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:base}
Both conventions require a base point ($u=0$), which is part of the data; this is a genuine feature of Caputo (memory) operators. For $\alpha<1$, $w(u)\to0$ as $u\to0^+$, so $|\kappa_\alpha(u)|\to\infty$ at the base point unless $\kappa$ vanishes there.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:chart}
\[
\Phi:\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\},\qquad \Phi(x)=\frac{x}{r(\theta(x))},\qquad g=\Phi^*\delta,
\]
where $\delta$ is the Euclidean metric.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:chart}
(a) $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $y\mapsto r(\theta(y))\,y$, and it maps the Gielis curve $\mathcal C=\{x:|x|=r(\theta(x))\}$ onto the unit circle.
(b) For $k\ge1$: $\Phi\in C^k$ if and only if $r\in C^k$. In polar coordinates $(\rho,\theta)$,
\[
g=r^{-2}\,d\rho^2-2\rho\,r'r^{-3}\,d\rho\,d\theta+\rho^2\bigl(r^{-2}+r'^2r^{-4}\bigr)\,d\theta^2 ,
\]
so, if $r\in C^k$, the coefficients of $g$ are $C^{k-1}$, and they are not $C^k$ unless $r\in C^{k+1}$.
(c) If $r\in C^2$, then $\Phi$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism and an isometry from $(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\},g)$ onto $(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\},\delta)$; hence $\mathcal C$ has $g$-length $2\pi$ and $g$-geodesic curvature identically $1$. If $r\in C^3$, then $g\in C^2$ and its Gaussian curvature vanishes.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(a) Since $r>0$, $\theta(\Phi(x))=\theta(x)$ and $|\Phi(x)|=|x|/r(\theta(x))$; hence $y\mapsto r(\theta(y))y$ is a two-sided inverse, both maps are continuous, and $|\Phi|=1$ exactly on $\mathcal C$.
(b) In polar coordinates $\Phi(\rho,\theta)=(R,\theta)$ with $R=\rho/r(\theta)$, so the regularity of $\Phi$ is that of $1/r$, i.e.\ of $r$. Inserting $dR=d\rho/r-\rho r'd\theta/r^2$ into $\delta=dR^2+R^2d\theta^2$ gives the formula. Its coefficients involve $r$ and $r'$, hence are $C^{k-1}$; the mixed coefficient $g_{\rho\theta}=-\rho r'r^{-3}=\frac{\rho}{2}(r^{-2})'$ is $C^k$ only if $r^{-2}\in C^{k+1}$, i.e.\ $r\in C^{k+1}$.
(c) By construction; isometries preserve length, geodesic curvature and Gaussian curvature.
\qed
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:transport}
If the governing exponent of a zero $\theta_*$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:regular}) equals $1$ --- for example for the rhombus $(4;1,1,1)$, or any $(m;n_1,1,1)$ --- then $r'$ jumps at $\theta_*$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:geom}); $\Phi$ is Lipschitz but not $C^1$ across the ray $\theta=\theta_*$, and $g$ has a jump discontinuity across it. If the governing exponent is smaller than $1$ (a cusp), $r'$ is unbounded near $\theta_*$ and $\Phi$ is not even locally Lipschitz. In these cases --- the ones the regularization is meant for --- the geodesic curvature of $\mathcal C$ with respect to $g$ is not defined in the classical sense; whenever it is defined ($r\in C^2$) it equals $1$, but this is encoded in $\Phi$: the non-smoothness of $\mathcal C$ has been moved into the metric.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:superelliptic}
We compare with \cite{Ozdemir2026} on two points.

(i) The superelliptic inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle_{SE}=r(t)^{-2}\sum_i\sigma_iX_iY_i$ \cite[eq.~(7)]{Ozdemir2026} depends on the parameter $t$ of a curve; it defines a Riemannian metric on the ambient space only if $t$ is expressed through the point, for instance $t=\theta(x)$ in the plane. With this reading and $\sigma_i=1$ it is the conformal metric $\hat g=r(\theta(x))^{-2}\,\delta$ on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$. For $r\in C^1$ the $\hat g$-length of $\mathcal C$ is $\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{1+(r'/r)^2}\,d\varphi$, which exceeds $2\pi$ unless $r$ is constant (numerically by $3.0\%$, $9.4\%$ and $38.6\%$ for $(4;4,4,4)$, $(5;7,7,7)$ and $(8;4,6,6)$). Hence $\mathcal C$ is not a unit circle for $\hat g$; a metric in which $\mathcal C$ is a unit circle is $g=\Phi^*\delta$ of Definition~\ref{def:chart} and Proposition~\ref{prop:chart}, which is not conformal ($g_{\rho\theta}\neq0$ where $r'\neq0$).

(ii) The star derivative $D^*=\mathcal{G}\circ D$ \cite[eq.~(23)]{Ozdemir2026} is not the derivative of the transformed curve. For the unit circle $\mathbf e(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ and $\sigma_i=1$, the transformed curve $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf e)(t)=r(t)\mathbf e(t)$ has velocity $r'(t)\mathbf e(t)+r(t)\mathbf e'(t)$, whereas $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf e')(t)=r(t)\mathbf e'(t)$; the two differ by $r'(t)\mathbf e(t)$, so $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf e')$ is not even tangent to $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf e)$ where $r'\neq0$ (for $(6;6,4,4)$ the angle reaches $19.5^\circ$, Figure~\ref{fig:star}). For a general curve $\mathbf c$ (denoted by another letter in \cite{Ozdemir2026}), the relation $\mathbf c^*_{SE}=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf c')$ of \cite[Proposition~1]{Ozdemir2026}, obtained ``by differentiating'', drops the corresponding term, and the constant-curvature statements of \cite{Ozdemir2026} (e.g.\ their Figure~5) concern $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf c')$ rather than the geometry of the curve $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf c)$. In \cite[Remark~2]{Ozdemir2026} the order ``differentiate first, then scale'' is motivated by interpreting $r$ as a metric radius; our objection is that the resulting vector field is not the velocity of any parametrization of $\mathcal{G}(\mathbf c)$.

This is why we base the present work on the chart $\Phi$, a genuine change of coordinates, and compute all differential invariants in the ordinary Euclidean sense.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:scaling}
Let $\mathcal C$ be a regular $C^2$ curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($C^3$ with $\kappa>0$ for the statement on $\tau_\alpha$), $c>0$, and let $c\,\mathcal C$ be its image under the homothety $x\mapsto cx$, the base point being mapped to the base point. At corresponding points
\[
\kappa_\alpha\longmapsto c^{-(1+p)}\kappa_\alpha,\qquad \tau_\alpha\longmapsto c^{-(1+p)}\tau_\alpha,
\]
that is, with exponent $2-\alpha$ in convention E and $1/\alpha$ in convention F.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
$\kappa\mapsto\kappa/c$, $\tau\mapsto\tau/c$, $u\mapsto cu$, and $w(cu)=c^p\,w(u)$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:param}
Let $n_2=n_3=n$. Replacing $(a,b)$ by $(ca,cb)$ multiplies $r$ by $\hat c=c^{n/n_1}$; it is the homothety of ratio $\hat c$, and $\kappa_\alpha\mapsto\hat c^{-(1+p)}\kappa_\alpha$. If $n_2\neq n_3$ and $c\neq1$, the ratio of the new and the old radial function equals $c^{n_2/n_1}$ at the zeros of $\sin(m\varphi/4)$ and $c^{n_3/n_1}$ at the zeros of $\cos(m\varphi/4)$; hence the parameter change is not a homothety centred at the origin and Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling} does not apply.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Write the bracket in \eqref{eq:gielis} as $A=A_{\cos}+A_{\sin}$ with $A_{\cos}=|\cos\frac{m\varphi}{4}/a|^{n_2}$ and $A_{\sin}=|\sin\frac{m\varphi}{4}/b|^{n_3}$. The new radial function is $(c^{-n_2}A_{\cos}+c^{-n_3}A_{\sin})^{-1/n_1}$; evaluate where $A_{\sin}=0$, resp.\ $A_{\cos}=0$, and use Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling}.
\qed
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:memory}
Let $r\in C^2$ be $2\pi/K$-periodic with $K\ge2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:periodic}), let $L$ be the length of the curve and $\ell=L/K$. Then $\kappa(j\ell+\xi)=\kappa(\xi)$ and
\[
\kappa_\alpha(j\ell+\xi)=\frac{\kappa(\xi)}{w(j\ell+\xi)},\qquad j=0,\dots,K-1,\ \ \xi\in(0,\ell).
\]
If $w$ is strictly increasing, which is the case for $0<\alpha<1$ in both conventions, and $\kappa(\xi)\neq0$, then $|\kappa_\alpha(j\ell+\xi)|$ is strictly decreasing in $j$. Since $\kappa\not\equiv0$, $\kappa_\alpha$ is not invariant under $u\mapsto u+j\ell$ for any $j\in\{1,\dots,K-1\}$: none of the rotational symmetries of the curve survives.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The rotation by $2\pi/K$ maps $\gamma(\varphi)$ to $\gamma(\varphi+2\pi/K)$ and preserves arc length and signed curvature; since $\nu$ is $2\pi/K$-periodic, $u(\varphi+2\pi/K)=u(\varphi)+\ell$. Thus $\kappa$ is $\ell$-periodic in $u$, and $w$ is strictly increasing because $p>0$ for $\alpha<1$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:basepeak}
By Remark~\ref{rem:base}, $|\kappa_\alpha|$ is unbounded near the base point whenever $\kappa(\varphi_0)\neq0$; for $(6;6,4,4)$, $\kappa(0)=-1/2$ and $\kappa_\alpha\to-\infty$ as $u\to0^+$. Comparisons between arcs must therefore be made at corresponding points, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:memory}, not via suprema over arcs.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:cesaro}
(a) The fractional curvature of a circle of radius $R$ is $\kappa_\alpha(u)=1/(R\,w(u))$, which is not constant for $\alpha<1$.
(b) A planar $C^2$ curve has constant fractional curvature $\kappa_\alpha\equiv\kappa_0>0$ if and only if its tangent angle is $\vartheta(u)=\vartheta(0)+\kappa_0P(u)$, i.e.
\[
\text{E:}\ \ \vartheta(u)=\vartheta(0)+\frac{\kappa_0\,\alpha}{\Gamma(3-\alpha)}\,u^{2-\alpha},\qquad
\text{F:}\ \ \vartheta(u)=\vartheta(0)+\kappa_0\,s_F(u)=\vartheta(0)+\kappa_0\Bigl(\frac{\alpha^2u}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}\Bigr)^{1/\alpha},
\]
and such a curve is unique up to rigid motion. For $\alpha=1$ both are circles. In convention F with $\alpha=1/2$, $\kappa(u)=\kappa_0u/(2\pi)$: the curve is exactly the clothoid (Euler--Cornu spiral). In convention E, with $\kappa_0=c/\alpha$ and $\alpha\to0$, $\vartheta\to cu^2/2$, so the clothoid appears only as a formal limit.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
(a) is \eqref{eq:scaling} with $\kappa=1/R$. (b) $\kappa_\alpha\equiv\kappa_0$ if and only if $\vartheta'=\kappa=\kappa_0w$, i.e.\ $\vartheta=\vartheta(0)+\kappa_0P$; use $\Gamma(3-\alpha)=(2-\alpha)\Gamma(2-\alpha)$, $P_F=s_F$, and $C_F=\frac18\,\Gamma(\frac32)^{-2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}$, $p_F=1$ for $\alpha=\frac12$. A planar curve is determined by $\kappa(u)$ up to rigid motion.
\qed
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:theta}
\[
\Theta_\alpha=\int_{(0,L]}\frac{d\vartheta(u)}{w(u)},
\]
whenever the integral converges (possibly improperly at $u=0$). For $C^2$ curves, $\Theta_\alpha=\int_0^L\kappa_\alpha\,du$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:dP}
Since $\kappa_\alpha=d\vartheta/dP$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:frenet}), $\int_0^{P(L)}\kappa_\alpha\,dP=\int_0^L\kappa\,du=2\pi$ for every simple closed $C^2$ curve and every $\alpha$, a trivial fractional turning-tangent theorem. $\Theta_\alpha$ instead weights the turning by the memory factor $1/w$, which emphasizes turning near the base point.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:theta}
Let $\mathcal C$ be as above, without corner at the base point, and let $\kappa$ be bounded on some interval $(0,\epsilon]$.
(a) If $p<1$, $\Theta_\alpha$ is finite; this holds for every $\alpha\in(0,1]$ in convention E and for $\alpha\in(1/2,1]$ in convention F.
(b) If $\kappa$ is continuous at $0$ with $\kappa(0)\neq0$ and $p\ge1$ (convention F with $\alpha\le1/2$), then $\Theta_\alpha$ diverges to $\operatorname{sgn}(\kappa(0))\,\infty$.
(c) If $\kappa\equiv0$ on $(0,\epsilon)$ (base point inside a straight edge), $\Theta_\alpha$ is finite for every $p\ge0$.
(d) For $\alpha=1$, $\Theta_1=2\pi$.
(e) If $|\kappa(u)|\le Mu^{q}$ on $(0,\epsilon]$ for some $M>0$ and $q>p-1$, then $\Theta_\alpha$ is finite; (a) is the case $q=0$. In particular, if $\kappa$ is $C^2$ near the base point, $\kappa(0)=0$, and $\mathcal C$ is symmetric about the normal line at the base point (so that $\kappa$ is even in $u$), one can take $q=2$, so that $\Theta_\alpha$ is finite for $p<3$, i.e.\ for every $\alpha$ in convention E and for $\alpha>1/4$ in convention F.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Shrinking $\epsilon$ if necessary, we may assume that no corner lies in $(0,\epsilon]$. On $(\epsilon,L]$ we have $1/w\le1/w(\epsilon)$ and $|d\vartheta|((\epsilon,L])\le\operatorname{TV}(\vartheta)<\infty$, so that part is finite. On $(0,\epsilon]$, $|\int\kappa/w\,du|\le\|\kappa\|_\infty C^{-1}\int_0^\epsilon u^{-p}du=\|\kappa\|_\infty\epsilon^{1-p}/(C(1-p))$ if $p<1$, which gives (a). In (b), $\kappa$ has constant sign and $|\kappa|\ge|\kappa(0)|/2$ on some $(0,\epsilon']$, so the integral over $(0,\epsilon']$ has modulus at least $\frac{|\kappa(0)|}{2C}\int_0^{\epsilon'}u^{-p}du=\infty$, while the rest is finite. In (c) the integrand vanishes on $(0,\epsilon)$. (d) $w\equiv1$ and $\int d\vartheta=2\pi$ by the theorem of turning tangents \cite{Hopf1935,DoCarmo1976}. (e) On $(0,\epsilon]$, $|\int\kappa/w\,du|\le MC^{-1}\int_0^\epsilon u^{q-p}du=M\epsilon^{1+q-p}/(C(1+q-p))<\infty$ because $q-p>-1$. If $\kappa$ is $C^2$ and even with $\kappa(0)=0$, then $\kappa'(0)=0$, and Taylor's formula gives $|\kappa(u)|\le\frac12\max|\kappa''|\,u^2$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:corner}
If the base point is a corner with exterior angle $\eta\neq0$, its contribution must be attributed either to $u=0$, where $1/w(0^+)=\infty$ for $p>0$, or to $u=L$, where it equals $\eta/w(L)$. The choice is arbitrary, so $\Theta_\alpha$ is not well defined and corners are not admissible base points. For the cornered test curves $(4;1,1,1)$ and $(4;2,1,1)$ the point $\varphi=0$ is a vertex, and we use the edge midpoint $\varphi_0=\pi/4$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:polygon}
For a regular $N$-gon with edge length $\ell$ and base point at an edge midpoint, the corners lie at $u_j=(2j+1)\ell/2$, $j=0,\dots,N-1$, each with exterior angle $2\pi/N$, and
\begin{align*}
\Theta_\alpha&=\frac{2\pi}{N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\frac{1}{w(u_j)}=\frac{2\pi}{NC}\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{2}\Bigr)^{-p}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(2j+1)^{-p},\\
\Theta^E_\alpha&=\frac{2\pi}{N}\,\frac{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}{\alpha}\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{2}\Bigr)^{\alpha-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(2j+1)^{\alpha-1}\qquad\text{(convention E)}.
\end{align*}
If $p<1$ and the perimeter $L=N\ell$ is fixed, then $\Theta_\alpha\to2\pi L^{-p}/(C(1-p))$ as $N\to\infty$, which is the value for the circle of perimeter $L$, with error $O(N^{-(1-p)})$; in convention E the error is $O(N^{-\alpha})$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The formula follows from Definition~\ref{def:theta}. Since $f(x)=(2x+1)^{-p}$ is decreasing, $\int_0^Nf\le\sum_{j<N}f(j)\le f(0)+\int_0^{N-1}f$, whence $\sum_{j<N}(2j+1)^{-p}=(2N)^{1-p}/(2(1-p))+O(1)$ for $p<1$. With $\ell=L/N$ this gives $\Theta_\alpha=2\pi L^{-p}/(C(1-p))+O(N^{p-1})$. For the circle, $\Theta_\alpha=\frac{1}{RC}\int_0^Lu^{-p}du=2\pi L^{-p}/(C(1-p))$ with $R=L/2\pi$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:helix}
Let $w$ be either weight, $P=\int w$, $\kappa_\alpha=\kappa/w$, $\tau_\alpha=\tau/w$, and $'=d/dP$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:frenet}.
(a) $\tau_\alpha/\kappa_\alpha=\tau/\kappa$. Hence the fractional general-helix condition $\kappa_\alpha/\tau_\alpha=\mathrm{const}$ \cite[Theorem~3.2]{HasYilmaz2023} characterizes exactly the classical general helices (Lancret's theorem \cite{Struik1988}).
(b) The fractional Izumiya--Takeuchi function satisfies
\[
\sigma_\alpha:=\frac{\kappa_\alpha^2}{(\kappa_\alpha^2+\tau_\alpha^2)^{3/2}}\Bigl(\frac{\tau_\alpha}{\kappa_\alpha}\Bigr)'
=\sigma:=\frac{\kappa^2}{(\kappa^2+\tau^2)^{3/2}}\,\frac{d}{du}\Bigl(\frac{\tau}{\kappa}\Bigr).
\]
Hence the fractional slant helices ($\sigma_\alpha$ constant) are exactly the classical slant helices of Izumiya and Takeuchi \cite{Izumiya2004}.
(c) If the derivative in (b) is taken with respect to $u$ while $\kappa_\alpha,\tau_\alpha$ are retained, one obtains $w\,\sigma$, whose constancy is not equivalent to that of $\sigma$ when $\alpha<1$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
(a) The factor $1/w$ cancels. (b) $\tau_\alpha/\kappa_\alpha=\tau/\kappa$, $d/dP=w^{-1}d/du$, and $\kappa_\alpha^2(\kappa_\alpha^2+\tau_\alpha^2)^{-3/2}=w\,\kappa^2(\kappa^2+\tau^2)^{-3/2}$. (c) The same computation without the factor $w^{-1}$.
\qed
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:HY34}
The condition obtained in \cite[Theorem~3.4]{HasYilmaz2023}, $(\tau_\alpha/\kappa_\alpha)'/\kappa_\alpha=\mathrm{const}$, is not the Izumiya--Takeuchi condition, even for $\alpha=1$: its derivation combines $\langle\mathbf{n}_\alpha,U\rangle=\cos\psi$ with $\langle\mathbf{b}_\alpha,U\rangle=\sin\psi$ (constant angle $\psi$, fixed unit vector $U$), which forces $\langle\mathbf{t}_\alpha,U\rangle=0$ because $\langle\mathbf{t}_\alpha,U\rangle^2+\langle\mathbf{n}_\alpha,U\rangle^2+\langle\mathbf{b}_\alpha,U\rangle^2=|U|^2=1$. The standard argument of \cite{Izumiya2004}, applied to \eqref{eq:frenetP}, gives $\sigma_\alpha=\pm\cot\psi$, i.e.\ Proposition~\ref{prop:helix}(b). A non-invariance of slant helices under Caputo scaling can only be obtained with mixed-parameter conditions such as (c); it is an artefact of differentiating with respect to a parameter other than the one in the fractional Frenet equations.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:convexbase}
The construction above needs a convex base. A curve $r=1/\rho(\varphi)$ is convex if and only if $\rho+\rho''\ge0$, because the numerator of~\eqref{eq:kappa} is $r^2+2r'^2-rr''=r^3(\rho+\rho'')$. For $(m;n_1,4,4)$ with $a=b=1$ we have $\rho=A^{1/n_1}$, $A=1-\tfrac12\sin^2(m\varphi/2)$, and a direct computation gives
\[
\rho+\rho''=\rho\,\Bigl[1-\frac{m^2}{n_1}\,\frac{3c+1}{(3+c)^2}+\frac{m^2}{16\,n_1^2}\Bigl(\frac{d\ln A}{dx}\Bigr)^2\Bigr],\qquad c=\cos(m\varphi),\quad x=\frac{m\varphi}{4}.
\]
Since $(3c+1)/(3+c)^2$ increases from $-1/2$ to $1/4$ on $[-1,1]$, the curve is convex if and only if $n_1\ge m^2/4$, and for $n_1=m^2/4$ its curvature vanishes exactly at the $m$ points $\varphi=2k\pi/m$. For $m=4$ this is the squircle; Figure~\ref{fig:helix_m} shows the helices over $(5;6.25,4,4)$, $(6;9,4,4)$ and $(7;12.25,4,4)$. The curves $(m;4,4,4)$ with $m\ge5$ are not convex ($\kappa(0)=1-m^2/16<0$), and neither are the test curves $(6;6,4,4)$ and $(5;7,7,7)$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
